effect_estimate.comment: 95% confidence intervals are not reported. Note an internal discrepancy: the Abstract claims 'sanitation governance and the quality of policies and monitoring were instrumental in shaping public attitudes towards participation', whereas in both Table 2 (F = 0.071, p = 0.790) and Table 4 (B = 0.087, OR = 1.091, p = 0.530) Factor 1 (Sanitation Governance) is statistically non-significant. Income differed across clusters in bivariate chi-square testing (Chi-Square = 9.632, p = 0.022, Table 3) but was non-significant in multivariable logistic regression (>5 million: B = 0.106, p = 0.835, OR = 1.112, Table 4).
effect_estimate.value: In binary logistic regression of citizen willingness to participate in community-based sanitation programs (Table 4; overall classification accuracy = 85.60%, Cox & Snell R² = 0.076, Nagelkerke R² = 0.129), Factor 3 ('Sanitation Infrastructure and Collaboration', comprising access to sanitation facilities, drainage systems, and treatment socialization) significantly predicted higher willingness to participate (B = 0.408, SE = 0.142, Wald = 8.293, p = 0.004, Exp(B) [OR] = 1.503), whereas Factor 1 ('Sanitation Governance', comprising regular monitoring, aesthetic considerations, and drainage socialization; B = 0.087, SE = 0.138, Wald = 0.394, p = 0.530, Exp(B) = 1.091) and Factor 2 ('Operational Sanitation Practices'; B = 0.103, SE = 0.141, Wald = 0.526, p = 0.468, Exp(B) = 1.108) were not statistically significant; female gender was negatively associated with willingness to participate (B = -0.776, SE = 0.319, p = 0.015, Exp(B) = 0.460) and bachelor's degree or higher education was positively associated (B = 1.229, SE = 0.551, p = 0.026, Exp(B) = 3.419). In cluster analysis (Table 2, N = 396), 'Adequate health standards citizen' (n = 296) vs 'Public health risk areas' (n = 100) differed significantly on Factor 3 (0.43280 vs -1.28110, F = 493.119, p = 0.000) and Factor 2 (0.08891 vs -0.26317, F = 9.464, p = 0.002), but not Factor 1 (0.00779 vs -0.02307, F = 0.071, p = 0.790).
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 6, Table 1; PDF p. 7, Table 2; PDF p. 8, Table 3; PDF pp. 9-10, Table 4

mechanism_certainty.comment: Observational cross-sectional survey subject to the non-experimental design ceiling of 2. Assigned 1 (documented association) because the analysis estimates cross-sectional statistical associations between respondent-reported perceptual EFA factors (Sanitation Governance/regular monitoring and Sanitation Infrastructure and Collaboration) and self-reported willingness to participate in sanitation programs / attitudinal clusters, without direct empirical observation of administrative or legal governance mechanisms operating in practice.

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines community participation and collaboration in urban sanitation programs ('participation', including citizen willingness to participate, drainage socialization, and treatment socialization under DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION) as well as sanitation governance and regular monitoring/oversight (Factor 1: Regular Monitoring loading = 0.836, under ENFORCEMENT). Note that 'Occupancy: Formal / Non-formal' in Table 3 corresponds to 'Occupation (1=formal worker, otherwise=0)' in H7 and Table 4 (employment formality, not housing tenure).

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Selected based strictly on the actual empirical design operationalized and reported in the paper: a quantitative cross-sectional survey analyzed with EFA, cluster analysis, chi-square tests, and multivariable binary logistic regression without an intervention comparator. Although the Abstract and Method nominally mention semi-structured interviews and field observations as a mixed-methods approach, zero qualitative methods of analysis, interview sample sizes, or qualitative empirical findings are reported anywhere in the paper, so it does not constitute a genuine mixed-methods empirical study under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1 (MMAT would only apply if judged solely on nominal self-description).

study_design.comment: Although the Abstract and Method nominally describe a mixed-methods approach (structured questionnaires, semi-structured stakeholder interviews, field observations, and educational outreach campaigns), no qualitative analysis procedures, interview counts, qualitative themes/quotes, observational results, or campaign evaluation data are reported in Result and Discussion; 100% of reported empirical results (Tables 1-4) come from a cross-sectional quantitative survey.
study_design.value: Cross-sectional citizen survey analyzed with Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA), cluster analysis, chi-square tests, and multivariable binary logistic regression (nominally described as mixed-methods with interviews and observations, but only quantitative survey data are reported)
